unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8: Entertainment and Media. In today's world, entertainment is everywhere. We watch films and documentaries on screens, listen to podcasts and radio shows, follow stories through books and graphic novels, and even create our own content. But how much do we think about the media we consume? How does a film tell a story? What makes a documentary different from a drama? Why do some commercials stay in our minds long after we have seen them?
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary file. Learn the unit words a few at a time and say the example sentences aloud.
Work through the Grammar file. Focus especially on participle adjectives, as they will appear throughout the unit.
Read the Story file, "The Scroll of Umbara", and answer the comprehension and discussion questions.
Work through the sections below: Key Vocabulary → Reading → Understanding the Text → Grammar Focus → Grammar Practice → Writing Workshop → Listening & Speaking → Check Your Learning.
Finish with the Check Your Learning self-assessment to see what you have achieved.

readings.title: Why Entertainment Matters
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Entertainment is not only about relaxation. It shapes how we see the world. A good film, a powerful documentary, or even a well-made commercial can change how people think and feel. In many East African and Somali communities, storytelling has always been at the heart of culture, from poetry and oral history to modern cinema.
Think about the different ways stories reach you in one week. A film at the cinema tells a story with actors, music and pictures. A television series tells one in short chapters, so that you come back for more. A documentary tells a true story about real people and places. A commercial tells the shortest story of all — a problem, a product, a smile — and it is designed to make you want something. Each form has its own rules, and each one is trying to make you feel something.
The people who make these stories choose every detail. A director decides which character we care about and which moment we remember. An editor decides how fast the story moves. A composer decides whether we feel excited or nervous before anything has even happened on screen. When you notice these choices, you stop being only an audience and become a thoughtful viewer — someone who can enjoy a story and, at the same time, ask who made it and why.
That is why learning about media belongs in an English course. Watching a film critically, describing what you saw, and explaining your opinion in a clear review are all ways of using language to think. And in a region with such a long tradition of storytelling, the thoughtful viewers of today are the storytellers of tomorrow.

readings.title: Screens, Stories, and the Art of Telling Tales
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Long before anyone owned a television or a smartphone, stories were told around fires. In the suburbs of ancient cities and in the open deserts of East Africa, people gathered to listen. A storyteller would stand, clear her voice, and begin. The audience was captivated. No one moved. No one spoke. The story held them like a spell.
Those early stories were the first form of entertainment. They taught lessons, preserved history, and brought communities together. A tale about a clever fox might teach children about honesty. A poem about a brave admiral might remind a whole town of its legacy. These were not just idle pastimes — they were the glue that held societies together.
Today, our stories come through screens. A film director is, in many ways, a modern storyteller. She decides how the tale unfolds, which characters we care about, and what feelings we carry away. Think of the last film you watched. Were you excited by the action? Were you moved by a sad moment? Were you frightened by a sudden twist? Those feelings did not happen by accident. The director, the actors, the music composer, and even the cartoonist who designed the opening titles all worked together to make you feel that way.
Documentaries tell true stories. A documentary filmmaker might travel to an archaeological site in the highlands, or follow a family through the harvest season, or show how a school in a spartan building with few resources produces inspiring students. Unlike a drama, a documentary does not invent characters. Instead, it uses real people, real places, and real events to make us think.
But not all media is created equally. Commercials, for example, are designed to persuade. They use bright colours, catchy music, and exciting images to make us want to buy something. A discerning viewer — someone who thinks carefully about what they watch — can spot the difference between a story that informs and a message that tries to sell.
Today there is a revival of local filmmaking in East Africa and across the Somali diaspora. Young directors are telling stories about their own communities, their history, their families and their dreams, and some of these films have been shown at international festivals. The tools have changed — from fires to screens — but the heart of entertainment stays the same: a good story, well told, still makes us feel something real.

readings.title: The Scroll of Umbara, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In the dusty highlands of Umbara, beyond the modern suburbs and into the foothills of the great ridge, an unusual archaeological site was uncovered. It began with a single shovel hitting stone, and ended with a full team arriving, their equipment buzzing with electrical hum.
Fourteen-year-old Sami stood behind the caution tape, wide-eyed. He was not supposed to be there. But his uncle, a hospitable and generous site guard, had whispered, "Only if you watch quietly and don't touch anything."
What they found would change the region's understanding of history.
The object was a scroll, sealed in a jar, hidden deep in what seemed to be a cemetery from an ancient dynasty. The symbols were strange — part unknown, part familiar. The experts argued.
"A lost monarchy, possibly pre-feudal," said one scholar.
"Maybe classical influence mixed with native customs," said another.
"But it's been partially damaged," added a third. "The outer layer was churned by centuries of soil."
The writing team prepared a translation. "Some parts have been proclaimed, others must be reconstructed," the linguist explained.
They never expected the scroll to tell a story — with power, belief, and consequence.
A few lines had survived in full:
"In the Year of Eternal Fire, the Scholar of Umbara led his students to the Valley of Memory. There, a rehearsal was performed daily beneath the Great Tree. But a rebellion led by the Confederacy sought to destroy them. The Scholar was later imprisoned. Let the light remain."
Back in town, the news spread quickly.
"The Scholar's story could be proof of racial and cultural conflict long before colonial rule," one historian said.
"A new legacy rises from the soil," wrote a reporter from Paris, where international universities tracked African finds closely.
Others warned of being too excited.
"Don't build utopias from old bones," warned an elder. "We must understand, not dream."
Sami asked his history teacher, Teacher Yasmin, "Was the Scholar real?"
"We don't know," she said. "But history is often built from characteristics found in ruins, not full stories. That's why archaeological work is so valuable."
"But he was imprisoned," Sami whispered. "Why would someone do that to a scholar?"
She looked at him kindly. "Sometimes, new ideas scare people. Especially if it threatens a system — like a feudal or royal one."
Weeks passed. A local exhibit was prepared.
"Show the dynasty timeline," the curator instructed. "Add captions to each symbol."
An artist painted the admiral of the old guard, towering over a scene of chaos. In the corner, the Scholar stood calmly, eyes closed.
One placard read: "The Scholar's teachings were never fully recorded. But his students preserved fragments of his customs."

readings.title: The Scroll of Umbara, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Another stated: "The movement was not just cultural — it was political. The Confederacy opposed his influence."
Sami stared at the map. One word whispered in his mind: terror.
He began writing in secret — building his own timeline of the Scholar's last days.
Using adverbs like "usually" and "often", he described the ceremonies performed at dusk.
Using the past passive, he wrote: "The scroll was hidden during the Confederacy's march. The Scholar was arrested. He was proclaimed a traitor. He was imprisoned."
He felt angry. But also fascinated.
Sami shared his writing with his grandmother.
"This is strong," she said. "But be careful. Tell the story — but don't become partial."
"Don't favour one side just because they seem gentle. Even peaceful leaders can make mistakes. That's what legacy means — it includes light and shadow."
The next week, Sami and his classmates visited the site officially.
They were told: "You may not touch artefacts. Do not step inside the cemetery. Observe only."
A researcher gave instructions: "Write a public report. Use imperatives and historical tone."
Sami's group wrote: "Document the Scholar's characteristics. List the systems — monarchy, Confederacy, feudal rule. Compare cultural and political causes of conflict. Include symbols from both classical and local tradition."
One student added, "Never forget what was done under orders."
Another added, "Include electrical sketches of the burial jars."
Sami drew a map with branching arrows: belief → rehearsal → fear → terror → legacy.
"Was imprisonment ever justified?" the teacher asked.
"No!" one girl said. "It's cruel."
"But if the Scholar was threatening the monarchy, they saw it as control," another said.
"But belief isn't a weapon," Sami replied. "He was trying to help."
"Maybe," said another. "But we weren't there."
They were told to write essays using evidence.
Sami's title: "Imprisoned Memory: Systems That Fear New Ideas."
In the final week, Sami stood at the exhibit as a student guide. Tourists asked him questions.
"What makes this story special?" one woman asked.
Sami answered, "Because we don't know everything. That makes it ours to explore."
He used clear verbs: proclaimed, imprisoned, discovered.
He pointed to the scroll. "That was partially burned — but its message lived."
One visitor from Merrimack, a teacher, told Sami, "In our schools, we don't teach about African scholars."
"You should," Sami said. "The Scholar was buried. But not forgotten."
On the last day, a candlelight tribute was held. It wasn't a ceremony. Just respectful.
"This land remembers. The scroll returned. We are not students of history. We are its writers."
And under the fading baobab tree, Sami whispered, "The Scholar was buried, but not forgotten — and now his story has a writer."

comprehension.question: What four ways of telling a story does the passage say might reach you in one week, and which of them is designed to make you want something?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A film, a television series, a documentary and a commercial; the commercial is designed to make you want something.
comprehension.explanation: The second paragraph lists the four forms and says the commercial is the shortest story of all, designed to make you want something.

comprehension.question: Where does the passage say the earliest stories were told, and how did the audience respond?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They were told around fires, where the captivated audience sat in silence and did not move or speak.
comprehension.explanation: The passage describes people gathering around fires while the captivated audience stayed silent.

comprehension.question: In part one of the story, where was the scroll found and how was it hidden?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The scroll was found sealed in a jar, hidden deep in a cemetery from an ancient dynasty.
comprehension.explanation: Part one says the scroll was sealed in a jar inside an ancient cemetery.

comprehension.question: What did Sami's grandmother mean when she said a legacy includes light and shadow?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She meant that a legacy holds both good and bad, so we should not favour only one side.
comprehension.explanation: The grandmother warns Sami not to become partial and to show both the light and the shadow.

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what turns a member of the audience into a "thoughtful viewer"?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Noticing the choices the director, editor and composer have made — enjoying the story while asking who made it and why.
comprehension.explanation: The third paragraph says that when you notice these choices you stop being only an audience and become a thoughtful viewer who asks who made the story and why.

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what three things did those early stories do for communities?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Early stories taught lessons, preserved history, and brought communities together.
comprehension.explanation: The text lists these as the reasons early stories held societies together.

comprehension.question: Why did the experts argue about the symbols on the scroll?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They argued because the symbols were unfamiliar and might point to a lost monarchy or a classical influence.
comprehension.explanation: The experts disagreed over whether the symbols showed a lost monarchy or a classical influence.

comprehension.question: What instructions were the students given before their official visit to the site?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They were told not to touch the artefacts, not to step inside the cemetery, and to observe only.
comprehension.explanation: Part two lists these imperative instructions given for the official visit.

comprehension.question: Why does the passage say entertainment is not only about relaxation?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because entertainment also shapes how people see the world and can change how they think and feel.
comprehension.explanation: The first paragraph explains that a film, documentary or commercial can change how people think and feel.

comprehension.question: How does the passage say a documentary is different from a drama?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A documentary uses real people, places and events, while a drama invents its characters.
comprehension.explanation: The passage states that a documentary does not invent characters but uses real events to make us think.

comprehension.question: What did the history teacher say history is often built from?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She said history is often built from characteristics found in ruins, not from full stories.
comprehension.explanation: Teacher Yasmin explains that ruins give only fragments, which is why archaeological work matters.

comprehension.question: What did Sami tell a visitor made the story special?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He said it was special because we do not know everything, which makes the story ours to explore.
comprehension.explanation: As a student guide, Sami tells a visitor that the mystery makes the story ours to explore.

comprehension.question: The passage says a film director is "a modern storyteller." In what ways is a director like an ancient storyteller?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Like an ancient storyteller, a director decides how the tale unfolds, which characters we care about, and what feelings we carry away.
comprehension.explanation: The passage draws the comparison directly when it calls the director a modern storyteller.

comprehension.question: Why does the passage say that commercials are different from other forms of media?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Commercials are designed to persuade rather than to inform or tell a story: they use bright colours, catchy music and exciting images to make us want to buy something.
comprehension.explanation: The passage separates media that informs from a message that tries to sell.

comprehension.question: What is happening with filmmaking in East Africa and the Somali diaspora?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A revival of local filmmaking has brought new voices to the screen: young directors are telling stories about their own communities, history, families and dreams, and some of these films have been shown at international festivals.
comprehension.explanation: The passage describes the revival and gives festival screenings as evidence that it is growing.

comprehension.question: The passage ends by saying "the heart of entertainment stays the same." What does this mean?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It means that although the tools change — from fires to screens — the human need to tell and hear stories does not: a good story, well told, still makes us feel something real.
comprehension.explanation: The closing line contrasts changing tools with an unchanging purpose.

comprehension.question: captivated (paragraph 1) — What do you think this means? What clue words help you?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Completely held or fascinated by something. The clues are the sentences that follow: no one moved, no one spoke, and the story held them like a spell.
comprehension.explanation: The surrounding sentences show the effect of the word rather than defining it.

comprehension.question: spartan (paragraph 4) — The text says "a spartan building with few resources." What does spartan suggest about the building?
comprehension.correctAnswer: That it is plain and bare, with very little in it. The phrase "with few resources" in the same sentence is the clue.
comprehension.explanation: You infer the meaning from the phrase placed beside it.

comprehension.question: discerning (paragraph 5) — The passage defines this word for you. What does a discerning viewer do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A discerning viewer thinks carefully about what they watch, and can spot the difference between a story that informs and a message that tries to sell.
comprehension.explanation: The passage supplies the definition inside dashes immediately after the word.

comprehension.question: revival (paragraph 6) — What is being revived? How do you know?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Local filmmaking in East Africa and across the Somali diaspora. The passage says the revival has brought new voices to the screen and that young directors are telling their own stories.
comprehension.explanation: You name what is revived and cite the sentence that shows it.

comprehension.question: The passage compares ancient storytelling to modern filmmaking. Do you think anything is lost when stories move from spoken words to screens? Explain your answer.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Open response. A strong answer takes a position and supports it — for example that the shared presence of an audience around a fire is lost, or that nothing is lost because film reaches far more people — and refers to the passage.
comprehension.explanation: There is no single right answer; credit the reasoning and the use of evidence.

comprehension.question: The passage says commercials "use bright colours, catchy music, and exciting images to make us want to buy something." Think of a commercial you have seen. How did it try to persuade you?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Open response. A strong answer names a real commercial and identifies the techniques it used, linking them to the persuasive methods the passage lists.
comprehension.explanation: There is no single right answer; credit the link between the example and the technique.

comprehension.question: Why do you think it matters that young East African filmmakers are telling their own stories, rather than having outsiders tell stories about them?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Open response. A strong answer explains that people who live a story know its detail and meaning, and that telling it yourself decides how your community is seen by others.
comprehension.explanation: There is no single right answer; credit reasoning about voice, accuracy and who controls the telling.

comprehension.question: The author writes that a good story makes us "feel something real." What is the most moving or exciting story you have ever seen or heard? What made it powerful?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Open response. A strong answer names a story and explains what produced the feeling — the characters, the ending, the music, or its closeness to your own life.
comprehension.explanation: There is no single right answer; credit the explanation of cause rather than the choice of story.

grammar.title: Participle Adjectives (-ed and -ing)
grammar.explanation: Participle adjectives come from verbs but describe nouns. The -ed form tells us how a person feels; the -ing form tells us what causes the feeling.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: A participle adjective is made from a verb and used to describe a noun, and choosing the right form changes your meaning. Use the -ed form for the person who feels something: "Sami was fascinated by the documentary." Use the -ing form for the thing that causes the feeling: "The documentary was fascinating." Study these pairs: the news was surprising, so everyone was surprised; the commercial was annoying, so the viewers were annoyed; the long film was tiring, so the audience felt tired; the ending was disappointing, so we were disappointed. Both positions are correct: you can write "an exciting film" before the noun, or "the film was exciting" after a linking verb such as be, feel, seem or look.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write "I was boring in the lesson", which really means they bore other people. If you felt the boredom, write "I was bored in the lesson."
grammar.memoryTip: Ask yourself, "Who or what has the feeling?" A person takes the -ed form; the thing that causes it takes the -ing form.
grammar.practice:
Choose the correct form: the (excited / exciting) news made everyone smile; after the long meeting the children looked (bored / boring); we were (amazed / amazing) by the effects; the instructions were (confused / confusing). Then write one sentence with an -ed adjective and one with an -ing adjective.

Answer key — Part A (choose the correct form): 1. the exciting news made everyone smile (the news causes the feeling, so use -ing); 2. after the long meeting the children looked bored (the children feel the emotion, so use -ed); 3. we were amazed by the effects (the people feel the emotion, so use -ed); 4. the instructions were confusing (the instructions cause the feeling, so use -ing). Part B (write your own -ed and -ing sentences) is open-ended — there is no single correct answer. Self-check instead: does your -ed sentence name the person who feels something (e.g. "I was tired after the trip")? Does your -ing sentence name the thing that causes the feeling (e.g. "The trip was tiring")?

More practice — Practice 1: choose the correct form. Say each full sentence. The documentary about archeological sites was fascinated or fascinating? After watching the long film, the children felt tired or tiring? The excited or exciting audience cheered when the hero appeared? We were amazed or amazing by the special effects? The plot of the film was very confused or confusing? Sami was inspired or inspiring by the Scholar of Umbara's story? The disappointed or disappointing fans left the cinema early? Have you ever seen a truly frightened or frightening scene in a film?

Answer key — Practice 1: fascinating; tired; excited; amazed; confusing; inspired; disappointed; frightening.

More practice — Practice 2: use each verb twice. Describe the thing with the -ing form, then the person with the -ed form. One, move: the new Somali film, and how you felt watching it. Two, annoy: the commercial, and how everyone felt about it. Three, amuse: the cartoon, and how your little sister felt. Four, interest: the story of the dynasty, and how the students felt. Five, frighten: horror films, and how you feel afterwards.

Answer key — Practice 2: the film was moving, so I was moved; the commercial was annoying, so everyone was annoyed; the cartoon was amusing, so my little sister was amused; the story was interesting, so the students were interested; horror films are frightening, so I feel frightened.

More practice — Practice 3: each sentence has one mistake with a participle adjective. Say it correctly. The film was very bored. I was very interesting in the documentary. The children looked very exciting before the show. It was a very tired journey across the desert.

Answer key — Practice 3: the film was very boring, because the film causes the feeling; I was very interested in the documentary, because you are the person who feels it; the children looked very excited before the show, because they are the ones feeling it; it was a very tiring journey across the desert, because the journey causes the feeling.

grammar.title: The Past Simple Passive
grammar.explanation: The past simple passive focuses on what happened rather than on who did it. We form it with was or were plus the past participle of the main verb.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use the past simple passive when the action matters more than the person who performed it, as in news reports, history and film reviews. Form it with was for singular subjects or were for plural subjects, followed by the past participle: "The scroll was discovered by the team"; "The documentary was filmed in Mogadishu"; "The film was watched around the world"; "The old films were restored last year." Add by when you want to name who did it: "The film was directed by a young Somali filmmaker." To make it negative, add not: "The admiral was not honoured." To ask a question, put was or were first: "Was the scroll damaged?"
grammar.commonMistake: A frequent error is dropping the participle ending, as in "The film was direct by a new studio." The verb must be a past participle: "The film was directed by a new studio."
grammar.memoryTip: Whisper, "It happened to something." Whatever received the action becomes the subject, followed by was or were and the past participle.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each active sentence in the past simple passive: the team discovered the cemetery; the curator displayed the scroll; millions of people watched the documentary; a young filmmaker directed the award-winning film. Underline was or were and the past participle in every answer.

Answer key: 1. The cemetery was discovered by the team. 2. The scroll was displayed by the curator. 3. The documentary was watched by millions of people. 4. The award-winning film was directed by a young filmmaker. Check that every sentence uses was (singular subject) or were (plural subject) plus the past participle, with the original subject now introduced by "by".
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Adverbs of Time and Frequency
grammar.explanation: Adverbs of frequency tell us how often something happens, from always down to never. Adverbs of time tell us when it happens, such as yesterday or later.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: The adverbs of frequency, from most to least often, are always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely and never. Place them before the main verb but after the verb be: "I usually watch a film on Fridays"; "She is always early." You can move sometimes to the start for emphasis: "Sometimes we go to the cinema." Adverbs of time say when: "We watched a documentary yesterday"; "The film was released last year"; "Then the credits rolled." These adverbs help you describe your media habits and explain routines clearly.
grammar.commonMistake: Placing the adverb after the main verb sounds wrong: "He plays often football." Put the adverb before the verb: "He often plays football."
grammar.memoryTip: Remember the order Always, Usually, Often, Sometimes, Rarely, Never with the sentence "Aunty usually offers sensible readers novels."
grammar.practice:
Choose the best adverb of frequency for each clue and write the full sentence: goes to the library most of the time; celebrate together every single time; forgets homework zero per cent of the time; watches documentaries frequently; has fruit about half the time. Then add one adverb of time to each sentence.

Answer key — Part A (best adverb of frequency for each clue): 1. goes to the library most of the time = usually (e.g. "She usually goes to the library."); 2. celebrate together every single time = always (e.g. "They always celebrate together."); 3. forgets homework zero per cent of the time = never (e.g. "He never forgets his homework."); 4. watches documentaries frequently = often (e.g. "She often watches documentaries."); 5. has fruit about half the time = sometimes (e.g. "He sometimes has fruit."). Your exact wording may differ, but the adverb must match the clue and sit before the main verb (or after "is/are/was/were"). Part B (add an adverb of time to each sentence) is open-ended — there is no single correct answer. Self-check instead: does your added adverb of time (e.g. yesterday, last year, then, later) answer "when", and does it sit naturally at the start or end of the sentence, as in "She usually goes to the library, but she went yesterday instead"?
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Imperatives in Instructions
grammar.explanation: An imperative gives a command, instruction or request. It begins with the base form of the verb and does not use a subject.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Imperatives make instructions clear in recipes, safety notices and reports, such as the report Sami's class wrote at the site. Begin with the base form of the verb: "Add symbols to your map"; "Show the dynasty timeline"; "Compare the two viewpoints." For a negative instruction, start with do not or don't: "Do not touch the artefacts." For a polite instruction, add please: "Please close the door quietly." Because instructions often come in a list, imperatives keep each step short, direct and easy to follow.
grammar.commonMistake: Adding the subject "you" turns an instruction into an ordinary sentence: "You add symbols." Drop the subject and start with the verb: "Add symbols."
grammar.memoryTip: Picture a coach on the touchline who does not shout "You run!" but simply "Run!" Short, direct and beginning with the verb.
grammar.practice:
Write five imperative instructions for a classmate visiting an exhibit. Include one negative instruction with do not, one polite instruction with please, and one that tells them to compare two objects. Begin every sentence with the base form of a verb.

This task is open-ended (your own five imperative instructions), so there is no single correct answer — use this model as a self-check instead. Model example, grounded in the unit's own exhibit scenario: "Look at the timeline first. Compare the two viewpoints on the information board. Please handle the artefacts carefully. Do not touch the display case. Show your notes to a partner before you leave." Check your own five sentences against the model: does every sentence begin with the base form of a verb and drop the subject "you"; is there exactly one negative instruction with do not/don't; one polite instruction with please; and one instruction that tells the reader to compare two objects?
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Combining Unit Grammar in a Film Review
grammar.explanation: Strong writers blend several grammar features in one paragraph, using the past simple passive and adverbs of frequency together so the writing sounds accurate and natural.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: In a film review you often combine the unit's grammar. Use the past simple passive to report facts: "The film was released last year and was filmed in Nairobi." Use adverbs of frequency to describe your viewing habits: "I usually avoid long films, but this one held my attention." Use participle adjectives to describe your reaction: "The opening was gripping and I felt moved by the ending." Read your paragraph aloud and check that each feature is used correctly before you continue.
grammar.commonMistake: Some writers turn every sentence into the passive, which sounds heavy. Mix active and passive sentences so the review stays clear and lively.
grammar.memoryTip: Plan, draft, then reread once for each feature in turn: the passive, the adverbs, and the participle adjectives.
grammar.practice:
Write a three-sentence film review that uses at least one past simple passive sentence, one adverb of frequency, and one participle adjective. Underline each feature and label it.

This task is open-ended (your own three-sentence film review), so there is no single correct answer — use this model as a self-check instead. Model example, grounded in the unit's own reading passage: "The documentary was filmed in Nairobi and was released last year. I usually avoid long documentaries, but this one held my attention. The ending was gripping, and I felt moved by the final scene." Check your own review against the model: is there at least one past simple passive sentence (was/were + past participle), one adverb of frequency placed before the main verb, and one participle adjective used correctly (-ed for the person who feels it, -ing for the thing that causes it)? Have you underlined and labelled each feature?

grammar.title: Editing and Proofreading Your Writing
grammar.explanation: Careful writers reread their work to check meaning, agreement, tense, punctuation and the joining words that link their ideas.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Editing means improving what you have already written. Read the paragraph aloud and check one feature at a time: are the sentences complete; do the subjects and verbs agree; is the tense consistent; are commas, full stops and speech marks correct; do joining words such as and, but and because link the ideas smoothly? Change only what improves the meaning, and be ready to explain why each change helps the reader.
grammar.commonMistake: Swapping words at random without checking meaning often makes writing worse. Explain the purpose of every change you make.
grammar.memoryTip: Follow four steps in order: read, notice, revise, then reread to confirm the meaning still holds.
grammar.practice:
Edit a three-paragraph response about a film or documentary. Mark six improvements, then explain in a sentence how three of them make your writing clearer or more cohesive.

This task is open-ended (editing your own three-paragraph response), so there is no single fixed answer key — use this self-check checklist instead, grounded in the unit's own rule: for each of the six improvements you mark, check whether it fixes (a) a sentence that was incomplete, (b) subject-verb agreement, (c) an inconsistent tense, (d) missing or incorrect punctuation (commas, full stops, speech marks), (e) a joining word (and, but, because) that was missing or wrong, or (f) unclear meaning. A good self-check explanation names which of these six areas each change addresses and says, in one sentence, why the change helps the reader.

writing.title: Writing 1: Writing a Film Review
writing.promptAndInstructions:
A film review is a piece of writing in which you share your opinion about a film. Good film reviews do not just say "I liked it" or "It was boring." They explain what the film is about, how it tells its story, and why you would or would not recommend it. Film reviews are an important part of media literacy because they help other people decide what to watch.
The structure of a film review
A well-organised film review usually has four parts:
Introduction: Give the film’s title, the director’s name (if you know it), the year it was made, and the genre (comedy, drama, documentary, animation, etc.). Write one sentence that gives your overall opinion.
Summary: Describe what happens in the film in 3–4 sentences. Do not give away the ending! Use the past simple passive where it fits ("The story was set in a small coastal town").
Your opinion: This is the most important part. Explain what you liked and what you did not like. Use participle adjectives to describe your feelings and the film’s qualities ("The acting was convincing", "I felt moved by the final scene", "Some parts were confusing").
Recommendation: Would you tell a friend to watch this film? Who would enjoy it most? End with a strong sentence.
Useful language for film reviews
Here are phrases you can use in each section of your review. Practise saying them aloud.
Introduction phrases:
"The film ______ was directed by ______ and released in ______."
"It is a [genre] film set in ______."
writing.modelText: A strong film review names the film, summarises the plot without spoilers, gives a clear opinion supported by participle adjectives, and ends with a recommendation.

activities.instructionsAndItems: Read six statements taken from the unit texts. Label each one fact or opinion, and explain your choice in a short sentence.
activities.answerSummary: A fact can be checked; an opinion states a belief. Accept correct labels with a clear reason.

activities.title: Activities 3: Design a Documentary Poster
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Design a poster for a documentary about local storytelling. Include a title, one persuasive sentence, and three unit words used correctly.
activities.answerSummary: Accept any poster with a title, one persuasive sentence, and three unit words used with correct meaning.

activities.title: Activities 4: Passive Voice Transformation
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Turn eight active sentences about films and history into the past simple passive. Check that each answer uses was or were with a past participle.
activities.answerSummary: Each answer should use was or were with a past participle, for example "The documentary was filmed in Nairobi."

activities.title: Activities 5: Evidence Hunt
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Find six important details across the unit texts. Record each detail and explain what it helps the reader understand about entertainment and media.
activities.answerSummary: Accept six relevant details, each with an explanation of what it shows the reader.

activities.title: Activities 6: Teach a Word
activities.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
activities.instructionsAndItems: Choose one unit word and design a short game or diagram that teaches its meaning to a younger learner. Include one example sentence.
activities.answerSummary: Accept any clear game or diagram that teaches the word's meaning and includes one correct example sentence.

quizzes.question: What does the word 'admiral' mean?
quizzes.options: A series of rulers from the same family over a long time. | A high-ranking naval officer who commands ships and sailors. | A short advertising message that tries to persuade you to buy a product or service. | An area outside a big city where people live in houses.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A high-ranking naval officer who commands ships and sailors.
quizzes.explanation: An admiral commands ships and sailors in the navy.

quizzes.question: Which word means a series of rulers from the same family over a long time?
quizzes.explanation: A dynasty is a line of rulers from one family, such as the Ming dynasty.

quizzes.question: What is a commercial?
quizzes.options: A short video or audio message that promotes a product. | An imagined perfect place where everyone lives happily and without any conflict. | A place where people are buried after they die. | An area outside a big city.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A short video or audio message that promotes a product.
quizzes.explanation: A commercial is an advertisement made to persuade you to buy something.

quizzes.question: Which word means 'simple and without comfort or luxury'?
quizzes.explanation: A spartan room is plain and bare, with no luxuries.

quizzes.question: What does 'utopia' mean?
quizzes.options: A high-ranking officer in the navy who gives orders to a whole fleet of ships. | An imagined perfect place where everyone is happy. | A young person who learns a trade from an expert. | A time when something becomes popular again.
quizzes.correctAnswer: An imagined perfect place where everyone is happy.
quizzes.explanation: A utopia is an imagined world where everything is perfect.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: Choose the correct word: The special effects in the film were ______.
quizzes.explanation: The effects cause the feeling, so we use the -ing form: amazing.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: Which sentence is written in the past simple passive?
quizzes.options: The team discovered the scroll. | The team is still discovering the old scroll in the cemetery. | The scroll was discovered by the team. | The team will discover the scroll.
quizzes.correctAnswer: The scroll was discovered by the team.
quizzes.explanation: The passive uses was or were with a past participle: was discovered.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: Which adverb of frequency means 'about half the time'?
quizzes.explanation: Sometimes means an action happens about half the time.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: In the passage, what does a 'discerning viewer' do?
quizzes.options: Believes every single message that is shown on the television screen. | Thinks carefully about what they watch. | Only watches cartoons and commercials. | Never watches any documentaries.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Thinks carefully about what they watch.
quizzes.explanation: The passage says a discerning viewer thinks carefully about what they watch.
quizzes.origin: Generated from this unit's reading passages

quizzes.question: In The Scroll of Umbara, where was the scroll hidden?
quizzes.options: Sealed in a jar in an ancient cemetery. | On a high shelf in the far corner of the town library. | Inside a modern film studio. | Under the seat of a city bus.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Sealed in a jar in an ancient cemetery.
quizzes.explanation: Part one says the scroll was sealed in a jar, hidden in an ancient cemetery.

teacherNotes.note: Model new language aloud, check meaning before independent work, use mixed-response modes, and give specific feedback on complete sentences, text evidence and vocabulary precision. Ensure an adult is present when learners use the AI tutor or record audio.

💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you help me practise saying these words and check my pronunciation?"
"Can you give me a sentence for each word so I can hear how it sounds?"
"Which of these words come from other languages I might know?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you help me find the answer to question 3? I am not sure where to look in the passage."
"Can you explain what context clues are and help me practise using them?"
"Can you ask me more questions about the passage to check I understood it?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"I keep mixing up -ed and -ing adjectives. Can you give me ten sentences to practise?"
"Can you explain the difference between 'I am bored' and 'I am boring'?"
"Can you check my sentences and tell me if I used the right form?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you give me five more sentences to practise participle adjectives?"
"I got question 5 wrong. Can you explain why the answer is 'frightening'?"
"Can you make a quiz where I have to choose between -ed and -ing?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you help me plan a film review? I want to review [name of film]."
"Can you check my film review and tell me if I used participle adjectives correctly?"
"Can you show me how to use the past simple passive in a film review?"
"I have never written a review before. Can you walk me through it step by step?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you be the filmmaker and I will be the journalist? Let us role-play the interview."
"Can you listen to me present my film review and give me feedback?"
"Can you help me prepare arguments for the screen time debate?"
"Can you ask me the listening questions and check my answers?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you help me pronounce these words correctly?"
"Can you use 'rehearsal' and 'revival' in sentences about everyday life?"
"What is the difference between 'eternal' and 'everlasting'?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you explain the difference between a monarchy and a dynasty?"
"What is a feudal system? Can you explain it simply?"
"Can you tell me more about English words that come from other languages?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you explain what 'utopia' means and where the word comes from?"
"What is the opposite of 'spartan'?"
"Can you use 'partial' in two different sentences?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you help me break down long words like 'archaeological' and 'characteristics' into syllables?"
"Can you explain what a cartoonist does in more detail?"
"Can you give me a sentence using 'churn' that is not about butter?"
💬 Ask Your AI Tutor
"Can you check my grammar answers and explain any I got wrong?"
"Can you give me more practice sentences for participle adjectives?"
"Can you help me rewrite active sentences into the past simple passive?"
"Can you test me on adverbs of frequency?"
